Chapter 3: The World Through Divided Eyes
Imagine walking through life feeling like you’re straddling two worlds at once. For someone living with a divided self, everyday life can feel confusing—sometimes even threatening. The most ordinary moments, like passing people on a city street, suddenly become loaded with uncertainty. Is that person staring at me? Can they read my thoughts? Am I even real, or just a character in someone else’s story?
Now, this isn’t just about being anxious or paranoid. What’s really going on is a deep uncertainty about what’s real—and about who you really are. One part of you tries to just live, to fit in, while another part hangs back, always watching, always doubting. It’s exhausting, feeling like you’re living two separate lives at the same time.
Sometimes, this split can get so intense that reality itself feels out of reach. A person might start to believe things that seem impossible to everyone else—like that they’re being controlled by someone else, or that their thoughts aren’t really their own. And here’s the thing: these beliefs aren’t just frightening because of what they say—they’re scary because they mean losing that basic sense of control over your own mind.
But even when someone’s deep in psychosis, there’s often a part of them that knows something isn’t quite right. Maybe they realize, deep down, that their beliefs sound strange. But that doesn’t make them go away. It’s like being trapped between two worlds, unable to fully believe either one.
Most people don’t realize just how much we rely on a steady sense of self to get through daily life. When that stability slips away, even the simplest tasks—picking out clothes, deciding what to say—can feel impossible. You might freeze up, unsure what to do, or swing between extremes just trying to find something that feels real.
And relationships? They get tough. You might worry that others can see right through you, or that they’re manipulating you somehow. It’s easy to pull away, or get defensive. But at the same time, there’s this deep longing for connection—for someone to really see you, and help you feel real again.
That’s where a therapist or helper can make all the difference. It’s not just about giving advice or reassurance. What truly helps is when someone’s willing to step into your world, to try and understand what it’s like to live with this split inside. That takes patience, empathy, and a real willingness to sit with uncertainty.
When someone feels genuinely understood, even for a moment, it can break through the isolation and unreality that come with psychosis. The goal isn’t to “fix” someone or erase their struggles. It’s about helping them rediscover wholeness—to know they’re real, that their experiences matter, and that it’s possible to trust themselves and others again.
